questions.title: What exactly is "hyperspherical energy" in OFT—cosine-sum or inverse-distance potential?
questions.question_body: In the OFT paper, hyperspherical energy is first described as the sum of hyperspherical similarity (e.g., cosine similarity) between all neuron pairs. But later it is defined as \(\text{HE}(\mathbf{W}) = \sum_{i\ne j} \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^{-1}\) with \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i = \mathbf{w}_i / \|\mathbf{w}_i\|\). For unit vectors, cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are related by \(\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^2 = 2(1 - \cos \theta_{ij})\). Are the authors using the inverse-distance potential as the actual HE, or are both forms used interchangeably? If inverse-distance is the real objective/invariant, can you explain why this choice (as opposed to a direct sum over cosines) and whether the invariance arguments rely on this specific form?

questions.title: Why does left-multiplying weights by an orthogonal matrix preserve pairwise neuron angles?
questions.question_body: The paper considers a layer with weights \(\mathbf{W}^0 = [\mathbf{w}_1^0,\dots,\mathbf{w}_n^0] \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\) and applies OFT as \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{W}^0\) where \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is orthogonal. I want to verify that for normalized columns \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i = \mathbf{w}_i/\|\mathbf{w}_i\|\), the pairwise angles are preserved, i.e., \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i^\top \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j = (\widehat{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_i^0})^\top (\widehat{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_j^0})\). Is the preservation due to orthogonality maintaining both norms and inner products, so normalization commutes with \(\mathbf{R}\)? Does this also hold for convolutional layers once they are reshaped into \(d\times n\) matrices?

questions.title: If OFT preserves all pairwise neuron angles, how can it still change the model’s behavior?
questions.question_body: OFT preserves the hyperspherical energy by keeping all pairwise neuron angles the same within a layer via \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\). Intuitively that sounds like preserving most of the layer’s "geometry." Yet the method achieves different behavior (e.g., stronger controllability) after fine-tuning. What is changing if all inter-neuron angles are fixed? Is the key that angles between neurons and the layer inputs \(\mathbf{x}\) are not preserved (since \(\mathbf{x}\) is not rotated), so the alignment of features with the input distribution changes even though neuron-neuron geometry stays the same? Some intuition or a simple example would help.

questions.title: Is OFT equivalent to rotating inputs by \(\mathbf{R}^{\top}\)? What are the implications across layers?
questions.question_body: Given \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{W}^0)^\top (\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{x})\), it seems OFT on a given layer is equivalent to rotating the layer’s input by \(\mathbf{R}^\top\). Does this interpretation hold in practice inside a UNet/Transformer block with residual connections and normalization? If multiple layers each learn their own \(\mathbf{R}_\ell\), does this behave like inserting orthogonal "preconditioners" between nonlinearities, or could some \(\mathbf{R}_\ell\) effects cancel out? Any guidance on how this interacts with layer norm and residual paths?

questions.title: Won’t stacking OFT matrices across layers cancel out and leave the network unchanged?
questions.question_body: If layer \(\ell\) uses \(\mathbf{W}_\ell = \mathbf{R}_\ell \mathbf{W}_\ell^0\), and the next layer uses \(\mathbf{W}_{\ell+1} = \mathbf{R}_{\ell+1} \mathbf{W}_{\ell+1}^0\), could there be regimes where the cumulative effect approximately cancels (e.g., if \(\mathbf{R}_{\ell+1}^\top\approx\mathbf{R}_\ell\)) so the overall function change is small? How do the nonlinearities and attention mechanisms prevent trivial cancellations, and is there any empirical evidence about learned \(\mathbf{R}_\ell\) matrices across depth (e.g., do they align or diverge)?

questions.title: Which norm is used in COFT’s constraint \(\|\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\|\le \epsilon\), and how is projection performed?
questions.question_body: COFT imposes \(\|\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\| \le \epsilon\) alongside orthogonality. Which norm is used here (Frobenius norm or operator/spectral norm)? When translating this to the Cayley parameter \(\mathbf{Q}\) via the Neumann approximation \(\mathbf{R} \approx \mathbf{I} + 2\mathbf{Q} + \mathcal{O}(\mathbf{Q}^2)\), how exactly is the projection implemented: do you project \(\mathbf{Q}\) onto a ball in the chosen norm each step? Any practical guidance for choosing \(\epsilon\) (or the corresponding \(\epsilon'\) on \(\mathbf{Q}\)) for stability without underfitting?

questions.title: Is the Cayley transform well-conditioned during training, and can it become numerically unstable?
questions.question_body: The orthogonal matrix is parameterized as \(\mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{Q}^\top = -\mathbf{Q}\). While \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}\) is always invertible for real skew-symmetric \(\mathbf{Q}\), could it become poorly conditioned as \(\|\mathbf{Q}\|\) grows, leading to unstable gradients? Do you regularize or cap \(\|\mathbf{Q}\|\) beyond the COFT constraint, and does the block-diagonal structure materially improve conditioning (beyond reducing matrix sizes)?

questions.title: What is the actual compute cost of Cayley parameterization compared to LoRA at training time?
questions.question_body: The paper focuses on parameter counts (e.g., OFT has \(\mathcal{O}(d^2/r)\) parameters for an \(r\)-block diagonal \(\mathbf{R}\)), but training-time cost also includes forming or solving with \((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})\) per block (potentially \(\mathcal{O}((d/r)^3)\) if naively inverted). How is this implemented efficiently in practice (linear solves, batched small inverses, or iterative methods), and how does wall-clock time compare to LoRA’s two low-rank multiplications in large SD v1.5 UNets?

questions.title: Why claim OFT is \(\mathcal{O}(d)\) when \(r=\alpha d\), but LoRA is \(\mathcal{O}(d^2+dn)\)? Is this comparison fair?
questions.question_body: The paper compares asymptotics assuming \(r=r'=\alpha d\), concluding OFT is \(\mathcal{O}(d)\) while LoRA is \(\mathcal{O}(d^2+dn)\). But in typical LoRA usage, \(r'\ll d\) is chosen to be a small constant. Could you provide an apples-to-apples comparison where both methods use the same parameter budget (e.g., equal trainable parameter counts), and report the resulting compute and quality trade-offs?

questions.title: How exactly is OFT applied to attention weights in Stable Diffusion?
questions.question_body: For fairness to LoRA, the paper says OFT is applied to the same attention weights. Concretely: which matrices receive \(\mathbf{R}\) (\(\mathbf{W}_q, \mathbf{W}_k, \mathbf{W}_v, \mathbf{W}_o\))? Is \(\mathbf{R}\) shared across heads or per-head? Is it shared across layers or unique per layer? Are block-diagonal \(\mathbf{R}\) blocks aligned with head dimensions? Some code-level clarification would help replication.

questions.title: How is OFT applied to convolutional layers with shape \(C_{out}\times C_{in}\times k_h\times k_w\)?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions interesting interpretations for conv layers and claims certain block structures are analogous to depth-wise transforms. How do you reshape conv weights \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{out}\times C_{in}\times k_h\times k_w}\) into a \(d\times n\) matrix to apply \(\mathbf{R}\)? If using \(r=C_{in}\) blocks, what are the exact block dimensions and how does this correspond to mixing within an input channel only? Could you provide a small example (e.g., \(C_{in}=2, k_h=k_w=3\)) to illustrate the mapping and the effect on the convolution?

questions.title: Does re-scaled OFT with a diagonal \(\mathbf{D}\) actually preserve \(\text{HE}(\mathbf{W})\)? Any side effects on normalization?
questions.question_body: Re-scaled OFT uses \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{W}^0\,\mathbf{D}\) with \(\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_n), s_i>0\), and claims that scaling does not change HE because columns are normalized when computing \(\text{HE}(\cdot)\). Can you provide a short proof that \(\text{HE}(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\mathbf{D}) = \text{HE}(\mathbf{W}^0)\)? Also, since \(\mathbf{D}\) changes pre-activations, does it interact poorly with LayerNorm/GroupNorm or require additional stabilization (e.g., constraints on \(s_i\) or learning rate)?

questions.title: What prevents the hyperspherical energy from blowing up when neurons coincide?
questions.question_body: Because \(\text{HE}(\mathbf{W}) = \sum_{i\ne j} \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^{-1}\), it diverges if \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i=\hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\). In OFT, this is avoided by construction since orthogonal transforms preserve the original distances. But in practice, with finite precision, could near-collisions cause numerical instability when estimating HE (e.g., for diagnostics)? Do you compute HE explicitly anywhere, and if so do you clip the inverse distances or add \(\delta\)-regularization?

questions.title: Why should preserving \(\text{HE}(\mathbf{W})\) correlate with preserving generative semantics?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that pairwise angles among neurons carry semantic structure, so preserving \(\text{HE}(\mathbf{W})\) should help preserve pretrained capabilities. Is there empirical evidence correlating \(\|\text{HE}(\mathbf{W})-\text{HE}(\mathbf{W}^0)\|\) with metrics like CLIP-I/CLIP-T or FID during finetuning? Could there exist weight configurations with identical HE but very different behaviors, and if so, why isn’t that a concern here?

questions.title: Toy autoencoder: what are the exact formulas for "magnitude-only" and "angle-only" feature maps?
questions.question_body: In the toy experiment, at test time you compare (a) the inner product used in training, (b) magnitude-only, and (c) angular-only activations, and show that the angular information nearly reconstructs the input. Could you specify precisely what (b) and (c) compute? For a filter \(\mathbf{w}\) and patch \(\mathbf{x}\), is (b) \(z=\|\mathbf{w}\|\,\|\mathbf{x}\|\) and (c) \(z=\cos \angle(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|\,\|\mathbf{x}\|}\)? If so, how is the decoder trained to handle these alternative feature maps at test time, given it only saw dot products during training?

questions.title: How does OFT enable controllable generation without extra inference modules like ControlNet?
questions.question_body: For controllable generation (e.g., edges or segmentation maps as control), ControlNet and T2I-Adapter add extra networks or adapters. The paper claims OFT adds no inference-time overhead. How are control signals injected into Stable Diffusion in OFT: additional input channels to the UNet, conditioning via cross-attention (e.g., tokenizing the control), or some other mechanism? If extra inputs are added, why is there no additional computation compared to the vanilla model?

questions.title: Details of the "control consistency" metrics for C2I, S2I, and L2F
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a control consistency evaluation: (1) For Canny-to-Image, how are edges extracted from generated images (which Canny parameters or edge detector), and how exactly are IoU and F1 computed and thresholded? (2) For Segmentation-to-Image, which segmentation model is used to parse the generated images, and are metrics (mIoU, mean/overall accuracy) computed on the model’s argmax outputs or probabilities? (3) For Landmark-to-Face, which landmark detector is used, how are faces aligned or cropped, and how is the \(\ell_2\) distance normalized (e.g., inter-ocular distance)? How sensitive are the reported gains to these choices?

questions.title: Under what conditions is \((\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0\) effectively low-rank, as suggested in the LoRA connection?
questions.question_body: The paper notes \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{W}^0 + (\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x}\) and says the update term is analogous to LoRA. However, \(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\) is generally full-rank if \(\mathbf{R}\ne\mathbf{I}\). When does \(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\) become low-rank in practice? Does the block-diagonal structure of \(\mathbf{R}\) imply anything about the rank of \((\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0\), or is the analogy purely conceptual rather than a strict rank constraint?

questions.title: Does OFT preserve angles only within a layer, and could cross-layer relationships be disrupted?
questions.question_body: HE is defined per layer as a function of pairwise angles among that layer’s neurons. If OFT preserves each layer’s intra-layer angles but different layers learn different \(\mathbf{R}_\ell\), could this disrupt cross-layer feature alignments that matter for diffusion models (e.g., encoder-decoder skip connections)? Have you measured any notion of cross-layer "angle structure" or is preserving per-layer HE empirically sufficient?

questions.title: How should we choose the number of blocks \(r\) in block-diagonal \(\mathbf{R}\)?
questions.question_body: The parameter count and compute scale with the number of blocks \(r\). Are there heuristics to set \(r\) relative to the layer width \(d\), data size, or task difficulty? Do you have ablations showing the stability/flexibility trade-off as \(r\) varies (e.g., convergence speed, final controllability, and risk of collapse)?

questions.title: What quantitative criterion defines "collapse" in the subject-driven experiments?
questions.question_body: The paper states that DreamBooth collapses after 2000 iterations while OFT/COFT remain stable. What metric is used to define collapse (e.g., reconstruction loss explosion, CLIP-I degradation, DINO score drop, or visual artifacts)? Is there a reproducible threshold or procedure to detect collapse across subjects?

questions.title: Does restricting to \(\det(\mathbf{R})=1\) (Cayley) hurt compared to allowing reflections?
questions.question_body: Cayley parameterization yields \(\mathbf{R}\in\mathrm{SO}(d)\) with \(\det(\mathbf{R})=1\). Do you expect any benefit from also allowing \(\det(\mathbf{R})=-1\) (reflections) by using, say, Householder products or the matrix exponential parameterization \(\mathbf{R}=\exp(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^\top)\)? Did you try alternatives (e.g., Lezcano’s parametrizations) and see differences in convergence or final metrics?

questions.title: Are you effectively performing Riemannian optimization on \(\mathrm{SO}(d)\), or is Cayley + SGD sufficient?
questions.question_body: Since \(\mathrm{SO}(d)\) is a Lie group, one could use Riemannian gradients/retractions. With Cayley, you instead optimize over \(\mathbf{Q}\) in Euclidean space and map to \(\mathbf{R}\). Does this introduce gradient bias or conditioning issues compared to explicit Riemannian methods? Any observed differences in practice on SD v1.5 when using exponential-map-based parametrizations vs. Cayley?

questions.title: How does OFT affect text alignment and classifier-free guidance (CFG) behavior?
questions.question_body: Because OFT rotates attention weights, could it systematically change alignment to text embeddings and alter the optimal CFG scale? Did you observe shifts in CLIP-T scores, required guidance scales, or prompt sensitivity compared to LoRA or DreamBooth? Any recommendations for CFG tuning when using OFT/COFT?

questions.title: Compositionality: when can multiple task-specific OFT matrices be multiplied without interference?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests a compositional potential: if tasks yield \(\mathbf{R}_1,\mathbf{R}_2,\dots\), one can form \(\mathbf{R}_{\text{combo}} = \prod_i \mathbf{R}_i\), which is still orthogonal. Under what conditions does this preserve performance across tasks (e.g., matrices commuting approximately, acting on disjoint subspaces, or small \(\|\mathbf{R}_i-\mathbf{I}\|\))? Any empirical results on composing two downstream finetunes (e.g., subject-driven + controllable) and measuring interference?
